Q466.L1t: Surveys across countries show that how much people say religion matters in their lives varies widely from place to place.
Q466.L2t: Pew Research Center asked people in many countries how important God is in their lives, and Turkey was among the countries surveyed in 2019.
Q466.L3t: In the 2019 survey, Turkey's share saying God plays an important role was well above 85 percent, far above the levels in most European countries.
Q466.L4t: Close to nine in ten Turks say God plays an important role in their life, the highest of the listed figures.
Q466.L2f: The 2019 survey on the role of God was conducted only in Muslim-majority countries and only among adults over 40.
Q466.L3f: In the 2019 survey, Turkey's share was in the high seventies, a little below the most devout Muslim-majority countries.
Q466.L4f: About four in five Turks say God plays an important role in their life, so the third-lowest listed figure is correct.

Q237.L1t: Early American presidents often argued about how the young republic should deal with the powers of Europe.
Q237.L2t: The phrase is often cited as a classic statement of early American neutrality in foreign affairs.
Q237.L3t: The line comes from an inaugural address delivered in March 1801, after a bitterly contested election, by the third president, who had also written the Declaration of Independence.
Q237.L4t: The speaker was the third president, the author of the Declaration of Independence, in his first inaugural address.
Q237.L2f: The phrase comes from an 1830 speech given at the opening of a new session of Congress.
Q237.L3f: The line comes from a twentieth-century president's address about neutrality as the United States faced a European war, in the era of the League of Nations.
Q237.L4f: The speaker was the twentieth-century president who led America through the First World War and championed the League of Nations.

Q251.L1t: Many baseball figures served in the military, and military service shaped parts of their careers.
Q251.L2t: A court-martial is a military trial for violations of military discipline, and insubordination is one of the charges it can address.
Q251.L3t: In 1944 an Army lieutenant stationed at Fort Hood refused an order to move to the back of a bus and was court-martialed, then acquitted, before he joined the major leagues in 1947.
Q251.L4t: The man acquitted was the player who broke baseball's color barrier in 1947, after his 1944 Army court-martial over a bus incident.
Q251.L2f: In the US Army, a court-martial is decided by a single judge, never by a panel of officers.
Q251.L3f: The player who was an Army captain in the First World War was court-martialed for defying a superior officer's orders and was cleared of the charge.
Q251.L4f: The Detroit Tigers outfielder who served as an Army officer in the First World War is the one who was acquitted at court-martial.
